title: Advanced drug delivery strategies for overcoming tumor-mediated molecular hijacking: Emerging nanotherapeutics, advanced biotherapeutics, and artificial intelligence.
authors: Kumar, Vivek; Batra, Priyanka; Das, Nivedita; Shende, Pravin
abstract: Recent advances in precision oncology fueled the development of nanotherapeutics,​ molecularly targeted drugs, engineered immunotherapies, RNA therapeutics, and smart biomaterials for more selective cancer treatment. However, long-term therapeutic responses remain restricted by interconnected adaptive mechanisms, including ABC transporter-mediated drug efflux, dysregulated signaling pathways, apoptosis evasion, immune escape, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and tumor microenvironment​ remodeling. In this review article, these processes are collectively framed as tumor-mediated molecular hijacking, describing malignant cell exploitation and microenvironmental pathways that promote multidrug resistance and therapeutic failure. The review critically examines nanotherapeutic and advanced biotherapeutic strategies to counteract these mechanisms, including functionalized nanocarriers, antibody-drug conjugates, CAR-T cells, tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy, immune checkpoint blockade, mesenchymal stem-cell (MSC)-based therapeutics, CRISPR-mediated genome editing, bispecific T-cell engagers, and RNA-based approaches. Particular focus includes drug-delivery elements such as tumour penetration, intracellular trafficking, controlled release, pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and critical formulation attributes, as well as translational challenges such as manufacturability, scalability, reproducibility, stability, safety, and regulatory feasibility. Emerging biofabrication approaches enable the fabrication of adaptive and personalized delivery systems, while artificial intelligence and machine learning are utilized as tools for structure-guided design, nanocarrier optimization, treatment-response prediction, and patient-specific digital-twin modelling. This paper combines tumor-mediated molecular hijacking with drug delivery technology at the forefront and translational aspects to create a comprehensive platform for clinically relevant precision cancer therapeutics.Clinical trial number: Not applicable.

title: An engineered probiotic yeast converts extracellular ATP into adenosine to alleviate experimental colitis.
authors: Liu, Huiye; Zhang, Mingxin; Wu, Weizhen; Deng, Qingyun; Li, Xiaofang; Ma, Rongwei; Bai, Lan; Huang, Bing
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic relapsing intestinal disorder characterized by mucosal inflammation, epithelial barrier disruption, and gut microbial dysbiosis. Excessive extracellular ATP (eATP) accumulates in inflamed intestinal tissues and amplifies immune activation through purinergic signaling, whereas adenosine generated from extracellular nucleotide metabolism exerts immunoregulatory effects. Here, we engineered the probiotic yeast Saccharomyces boulardii to sense eATP and convert it into adenosine through a CRISPR-engineered dual-enzyme pathway consisting of apyrase and 5'-nucleotidase. The engineered strain showed ATP-responsive pathway activation and efficiently generated adenosine from eATP, allowing extracellular nucleotide metabolism to be modulated in inflammatory settings. Oral administration of this strain significantly alleviated disease severity in acute dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis and showed beneficial effects in a repeated-DSS model, improved barrier-related epithelial features, reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production, and supported mucosal recovery. Integrated microbiome and transcriptome analyses further showed partial restoration of gut microbial community structure, partial recovery of predicted microbial purine-related pathways, and attenuation of mucosal T-cell activation. Together, these findings indicate that engineered Saccharomyces boulardii can regulate extracellular purine metabolism in the inflamed gut and provide a microbial strategy for modulating intestinal inflammation.

title: CRISPR/Cas9 Editing of Starch Branching Enzyme Genes Remodels Starch Structure and Improves Nutritional Quality in Sweet Potato.
authors: Fan, Weijuan; Li, Yanshen; Xu, Ziyin; Nie, Haozhen; Gao, Yusen; Yang, Jun; Wang, Hongxia
abstract: Starch branching enzymes (SBEs) play a central role in determining amylopectin architecture and starch functionality, yet their contribution to starch nutritional quality and crop performance in sweet potato remains unclear. In this study, CRISPR/Cas9 was used to target SBEI and SBEII in sweet potato, generating lines with reduced SBE activity. Edited lines showed markedly increased amylose and resistant starch contents compared with the wild type. Amylopectin chain length analysis revealed a decrease in short chains and a relative increase in longer chains, indicating substantial remodeling of branch structure. Microscopic observations further showed reduced birefringence and structural irregularities in starch granules. These structural changes resulted in altered physicochemical properties, including decreased swelling power and solubility, elevated gelatinization temperature, and modified pasting behavior. In vitro digestion assays demonstrated significantly reduced starch digestibility and lower predicted glycemic index values. Whole-genome resequencing confirmed the stable integration of T-DNA and predicted limited insertion-associated effects, further supporting that the improved starch traits were primarily derived from targeted SBE editing. Importantly, storage root yield remained comparable to that of wild-type plants. Collectively, these results demonstrate that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated SBE editing effectively improves starch nutritional quality without compromising yield, providing a promising strategy for developing health-oriented sweet potato varieties.

title: Noncanonical enhancers control gene expression and cell fate in human pluripotent stem cells.
authors: Cao, Yang; Dovgusha, Oleksandr; Ebrahimi, Ayyub; Cruz, Carmela Rieline V; Bevan, Stephen; Widmer, Lukas; Torabi, Fereshteh; Kurlovich, Julia; Rodriguez-Polo, Ignacio; Khan, Soumen; Patel, Manthan; Shiels, Oliver T; Pradeepa, Madapura M; Flynn, Sean M; Gunesdogan, Ufuk; Schoenfelder, Stefan
abstract: Enhancers are key gene regulatory elements that ensure the precise spatiotemporal execution of developmental gene expression programs. However, recent findings indicate that current approaches to identify enhancers may not capture the full repertoire of active enhancers in mammalian genomes. Here, we combine massively parallel enhancer assays with chromatin structure and transcriptome profiling to functionally annotate enhancers genome-wide in human induced pluripotent stem cells. We find that a substantial fraction ( approximately 40%) of accessible chromatin regions with enhancer function lack key features associated with active enhancers, including the active enhancer mark histone H3 lysine-27 acetylation and enhancer-associated RNAs. Perturbation of this class of noncanonical enhancers by CRISPR-mediated epigenome editing or deletion results in decreased levels of target gene expression and, in one instance, loss of pluripotent stem cell characteristics. Collectively, our data demonstrate enhancer activity for a class of gene regulatory elements that had, until now, only been associated with a neutral or inactive status, challenging current models of enhancer function.

title: Population structure of group B Streptococcus from semen reveals virulent and resistant lineages with implications for surveillance.
authors: Merces, Ana Clarisse; Costa, Natalia Silva; Oliveira, Laura Maria Andrade; Botelho, Ana Caroline Nunes; Barros, Laylla Graca; Silva, Luisa de Miranda Basto; Teixeira, Lucia Martins; Fracalanzza, Sergio Eduardo Longo; Khan, Uzma; Bentley, Stephen; Jamrozy, Dorota; Pinto, Tatiana Castro Abreu
abstract: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is a major agent of perinatal infections. Although extensively studied as a pathogen in pregnant individuals and neonates, little is known about GBS from male adults, despite occasional reports of its occurrence in semen. We characterized 120 GBS isolates obtained from semen samples in Brazil between 2017 and 2022 to determine serotypes, antimicrobial susceptibility profile, virulence-associated determinants, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) diversity and phylogenetic relationships with isolates from other clinical sources. Serotype V was the most frequent, followed by Ia, Ib, III, II and IV. Resistance was observed for tetracycline (84.1%), erythromycin (30.8%), levofloxacin (8.3%) and 12.5% exhibited multidrug resistance (MDR). The most common sequence types (STs) were ST1, ST144 and ST19. The isolates clustered into five major clonal complexes (CC1, CC17, CC19, CC23 and CC24) and six singletons. Serotypes, antimicrobial resistance and virulence-associated determinants markers varied across CCs. Resistance determinants detected included tetM, mefA, msrD, ermA and ermB. Levofloxacin-resistant isolates contained mutations in gyrA and/or parC and were predominantly linked to the serotype V/ST19 lineage. All isolates except one carried at least one alpha-like protein (Alp) gene. Phylogenetic analysis of isolates from semen, rectovaginal samples, urine and invasive infections showed that isolates clustered according to CC regardless of clinical source. CRISPR1 analysis revealed intra-clonal diversity, as isolates within the same CC displayed different CRISPR compositions. These findings indicate that GBS isolates recovered from semen belong to established GBS lineages also identified in other clinical sources and support the co-circulation of GBS lineages across different human niches.

title: Structure-activity relationship and antibacterial mechanism of saponins from quinoa husks against Bacillus cereus and their application in rice.
authors: Han, Chengcheng; Wang, Yan; Yang, Lijing; He, Yi; Song, Linmeng; Zhang, Ruoyu; Lu, Hao; Xue, Peng
abstract: Bacillus cereus (B. cereus) is a major foodborne pathogen and a persistent food safety concern. Although plant saponins are promising natural antimicrobials, the antibacterial activity of Chenopodium quinoa Willd. husk saponins against B. cereus remains poorly understood. This study investigated the structure-activity relationship and antibacterial mechanism of quinoa husk saponins against B. cereus and evaluate their potential application in rice preservation. In this study, less polar saponins exhibited stronger antibacterial activity against B. cereus than more polar saponins among the twelve tested saponins. Among them, phytolaccagenic acid (Q8), isolated from quinoa husks for the first time, exhibited the strongest antibacterial activity, with minimum inhibitory concentration and minimum bactericidal concentration values of 125 and 1000 mug/mL, respectively. Q8 showed low cytotoxicity in GES-1 and effectively inhibited B. cereus proliferation and spoilage in rice. Further assays showed that Q8 disrupted membrane stability, causing membrane potential dissipation, protein leakage, cell deformation, and reactive oxygen species accumulation. Metabolomic and lipidomic analyses revealed Q8 mainly affected glutathione metabolism, cysteine and methionine metabolism, fatty acid degradation, and glycerophospholipid/glycerolipid metabolism. Molecular docking, RT-qPCR, CRISPR-Cas9 knockout, and genetic complementation analyses confirmed that squalene-hopene cyclase is essential for hopanoid biosynthesis, and hopanoids protect B. cereus against Q8-induced membrane damage. These findings support the potential application of quinoa saponins as natural antibacterial agents in food systems.

title: Discovery and Optimization of Anticancer Dibenzothiazepinones That Target the Ribosome Biogenesis Factor NVL.
authors: Tao, Ye; Guo, Holly H; Cruz, Victor E; Reddy, Divya; Leach, Ashley; Williams, Noelle S; Aurora, Arin B; Khivansara, Vishal; Han, Yan; Erzberger, Jan P; Nijhawan, Deepak; De Brabander, Jef K
abstract: Using inducible forward genetics, we recently discovered a dibenzothiazepinone (1) with activity against cancer cells via inhibition of the ribosome biogenesis factor NVL (nuclear valosin-containing protein-like). Herein, we delineate a comprehensive structure-activity relationship (SAR) study that explores the structural space surrounding the dibenzothiazepinone scaffold. A series of 115 analogs were synthesized and evaluated for activity against the colorectal cancer cell line HCT116 and counter-screened against cells CRISPR engineered to express a compound-resistant mutation in NVL. Our initial medicinal chemistry-driven campaign focused on improving potency, metabolic stability, and in vivo exposure and clearance. A fluorescence polarization assay with recombinant human NVL established a correlation between NVL-binding and antiproliferative activity. Cryo-EM structures of human NVL with select inhibitors revealed a binding mode that is consistent with the SAR data. This study led to the in vivo analog 100 (MM927), which we reported to suppress tumor growth in vivo without detectable toxicity via targeting the NVL.

title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA.
authors: Donaldson, Gregory P; Lima Dos Reis, Gabriella; Saad, Marwa; Wichmann, Christopher; Mamede, Izabela; Chen, Guo; Harrer, Caroline E; DelGaudio, Nicole L; Zhang, Dayu; Aydin, Begum; Castro, Tiago B R; Grivennikov, Sergei I; Reis, Bernardo S; Liu, Elise G; Eisenbarth, Stephanie C; Birsoy, Kivanc; Tavazoie, Sohail F; Stadtmueller, Beth M; Victora, Gabriel D; Mucida, Daniel
abstract: Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody isotype produced by mammals, and has a specialized role in mucosal homeostasis(1). IgA is constantly secreted into the intestinal lumen and binds to commensal microorganisms to regulate their colonization and function(2,3), with unclear implications for health. IgA deficiency is common in humans, but difficult to study, because of its complex aetiology and comorbidities(4-8). Here we use genetically and environmentally controlled mice to show that various models of IgA deficiency result in increased susceptibility to several models of endogenous colorectal cancer. Cellular and molecular analyses revealed that, in the absence of IgA, colonic epithelial cells induce antibacterial factors and accelerate cell cycling in response to the microbiota. Oral treatment with IgA was sufficient to reduce steady-state proliferation and protect mice from tumours; however, this function was due to the structure of the antibody rather than to binding specificity. In a reductionist culture system, IgA directly suppressed epithelial growth. Co-immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and targeted CRISPR screening identified DMBT1 as an IgA-binding epithelial surface protein that is required for IgA-mediated suppression of proliferation. Together, IgA and DMBT1 tune the normal cycling of absorptive colonocyte progenitors. In IgA-knockout mice, deleting the transmembrane and cytoplasmic signalling portions of DMBT1 was sufficient to reverse both the increased epithelial cell proliferation and the increased tumour susceptibility seen in these mice. These experiments establish a homeostatic function for IgA in tempering physiological epithelial responses to the microbiota to maintain mucosal health.

title: Functional characterization of os9 reveals its role in zebrafish developmental regulation.
authors: Xie, Qiuting; Wu, Lingxin; Wu, Jiayi; He, Meiling; Li, Wenhua
abstract: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated degradation (ERAD) plays a critical role in maintaining proteostasis during development, yet its in vivo functions remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the role of os9, a key ERAD component, in zebrafish development. Sequence and protein-protein interaction analyses revealed that Os9 is highly conserved across vertebrates and participates in ER protein quality control. Using CRISPR/Cas9, we generated os9 knockout zebrafish lines and found that loss of os9 leads to developmental defects with incomplete penetrance. Affected os9 mutant larvae exhibited cardiovascular abnormalities, including pericardial edema, disrupted cardiac structure, and abnormal erythrocyte distribution. In addition, affected os9 mutants displayed microphthalmia with reduced retinal size, while retinal lamination was largely preserved. Ultrastructural analysis revealed pronounced ER dilation and mitochondrial disruption in photoreceptor cells, accompanied by downregulation of photoreceptor marker genes and impaired photoreceptor development. Furthermore, os9 deficiency was associated with increased apoptosis and oxidative stress, as evidenced by elevated Caspase 9 activity, altered expression of apoptosis-related genes, and imbalance of antioxidant markers. Transcriptome analysis of affected os9 mutants revealed extensive gene expression reprogramming, characterized by enrichment of stress- and apoptosis-related pathways and suppression of metabolic and redox-associated processes. Notably, genes involved in protein processing in ER were significantly upregulated, while pathways related to retinol metabolism and phototransduction were downregulated. Collectively, these findings suggest that os9 is required for maintaining cellular homeostasis during zebrafish development and that its loss leads to ER stress, oxidative stress, apoptosis, and tissue-specific developmental defects, particularly in the cardiovascular system and retina.

title: The recognition pathway: reconceiving inventorship and obviousness for iterative CRISPR-AI convergence.
journal: Journal of law and the biosciences
abstract: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats -Artificial Intelligence (CRISPR-AI) convergence generate therapeutic candidates via iterative human-machine workflows that disrupt the inventorship criterion of patent law based on conception. In CRISPR-AI studies, AI systems suggest thousands of guide RNAs or Cas variants; human researchers select, confirm, and optimize them via experimental feedback loops that conceal the locus of conception. The existing patent doctrine, which demands a clear and final concept in the human mind, fails to align with inventions in which AI comes up with solutions that human researchers had not anticipated. This Article advances a recognition pathway for CRISPR-AI inventorship that maintains the natural-person baseline while attributing inventorship to humans who exercise claim-defining technical judgment in identifying patentable value within AI outputs. The Article reconceives the person having ordinary skill in the art standard for AI-enhanced biotechnology, rejecting both inflexible pre-AI baselines and the 'computer having ordinary skill in the art' proposal. A five-factor test is employed to assess AI-generated CRISPR inventions on non-obviousness in terms of problem structure, predictability of solutions, and quality of human judgment. The framework provides a computational biotechnology human-accountability grammar that is administrable, but not legally granted to machines.

title: Decoupled Signal Transduction via a Non-Copper Laccase Mimic for CRISPR-Based Electrochemical Detection of Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
authors: Li, Huimin; Zhou, Ya; Yan, Yifan; Ye, Jing; Dong, Xuefei; Chen, Mengjie; Meng, Tian; Jiao, Dongxu; Wang, Dewen; Zhu, Liping; Yang, Xiurong
abstract: Laccase-mimicking nanozymes have been overwhelmingly copper-dependent, and largely confined to environmental contexts, with clinical translation remaining unrealized. Here, we depart from this paradigm by designing a non-copper nanozyme, Mn-Trp NR, assembled through manganese-tryptophan coordination. Spectroscopic and theoretical analyses show that tryptophan coordination finely modulates the Mn electronic structure, strengthening O2 adsorption and lowering the reaction barrier, thereby conferring laccase-like activity, substrate affinity, and stability superior to the native enzyme. To overcome broad-substrate promiscuity that precludes specific biomarker recognition, we decoupled signal transduction from target identification: Mn-Trp NR serves as a universal amplifier, whereas CRISPR/Cas12a confers high specificity. Accordingly, a cascaded electrochemical biosensor was built on a DNA triangular prism integrating catalytic hairpin assembly, hybridization chain reaction, and CRISPR/Cas12a activation. The platform detects hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) biomarkers microRNA-122 (miRNA-122) and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) with limits of 11.98 aM and 10.31 fg/mL, respectively, in a streamlined 160 min, two-step procedure. In clinical sera, the biosensor perfectly distinguishes HCC patients from healthy donors (AUC = 1.00) and agrees strongly with benchmark methods (RT-qPCR for miRNA-122, ELISA for AFP, R2 > 0.97). By expanding laccase-mimic synthesis beyond copper via ligand-field engineering and establishing a decoupled architecture that reconciles broad-spectrum catalysis with high-specificity recognition, this work provides a generalizable strategy for deploying nanozymes in precision diagnostics.

title: A quantitative and visual detection probe based on isothermal nucleic acid amplification coupled with CRISPR/Cas12a system (INACS) for miR155 detection.
authors: Ma, Yunsu; Li, Jing; Jin, Xiaojuan; Liu, Sunan; Chang, Yajuan; Lin, Tongze; Zhang, Chengchen; Zhu, Ling
abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) have emerged as ideal biomarkers for early clinical diagnosis. Achieving the accurate detection of miRNAs plays a critical role for assuring its implementation in their clinical applications. In this study, we developed a dual-signal amplified ultrasensitive fluorescent sensing platform for miR155 detection by coupling isothermal nucleic acid amplification with the CRISPR/Cas12a system (INACS). Using a hairpin nucleic acid probe (HP) as the substrate, the system specifically recognizes the target miR155, triggering the opening of the hairpin loop structure. Subsequently, under the catalysis of Bst DNA polymerase, target gene amplification produces dsDNA with a specific sequence. This dsDNA activates the trans-cleavage activity of Cas12a, which cleaves reporter strands labeled with quencher and fluorescent groups, restoring the fluorescence signal. The fluorescence intensity is proportional to miR155 concentration, exhibiting a strong linear relationship between fluorescence intensity ratio and the logarithm of miR155 concentration over the range of 0.5-50 pM (r = 0.9961). By integrating nucleic acid amplification with CRISPR/Cas12a amplification, INACS achieves high sensitivity, excellent selectivity, and a detection limit as low as 34.46 fM. INACS was successfully applied to human serum samples, revealing elevated miR155 levels in breast cancer patients compared to non-cancer controls. Moreover, INACS was adapted for semi-quantitative detection using lateral flow assay (LFA) test strips. Results were assessed by naked-eye color comparison, facilitating rapid onsite auxiliary diagnosis of breast cancer. The LFA outcomes were consistent with serum fluorescence measurements, enabling efficient and user-friendly visual detection. This work thus provides a promising tool for early clinical diagnosis.
